shared.commonMistake: Read the console under the preview first. One red error stops the rest of the script, so fix the first error before anything else.
shared.bestPractice: Write the smallest piece of {topic} code that works, run it, then improve names and structure once every check passes.

js-console-log.title: Say hello
js-console-log.summary: console.log prints a value in the console under the preview. It is the quickest way to see what your code is doing.
js-console-log.objective: Print the exact text Hello, world! to the console with console.log.
hints: Text in JavaScript goes between quotes, and console.log prints whatever you give it.
Call console.log and put the text Hello, world! inside the parentheses, in quotes.
`console.log('Hello, world!')`

js-const.title: Store a value
js-const.summary: A variable gives a value a name so you can use it again. const creates a name that always points to the same value.
js-const.objective: Declare a constant named name that holds your first name as text, then print name to the console.
hints: A variable is a label for a value. Declare it once, then use its name anywhere after.
Write const, the name name, then = and your first name in quotes. Then pass name to console.log, without quotes.
`const name = 'Ada'` then `console.log(name)`
js-const.commonMistake: console.log('name') prints the word name, not the value. Quotes make text; without quotes, JavaScript uses the variable.
checks: The console shows the value of name

js-let.title: Change a value
js-let.summary: let creates a variable that can get a new value later. Use it only when a value really needs to change.
js-let.objective: Declare score with let and start it at 0. On a later line, add 10 to score, then print score.
hints: A const cannot be reassigned, so a changing score needs the other keyword.
Start with let score = 0, then reassign it with score = score + 10 or the shorter score += 10.
`let score = 0`, then `score += 10`, then `console.log(score)`
js-let.bestPractice: Use const by default and let only when the value must change, like a score or a counter. It tells readers which values move.
checks: score is updated after it is declared

js-numbers.title: Do the math
js-numbers.summary: JavaScript does arithmetic with +, -, * and /. Storing results in well named constants keeps calculations readable.
js-numbers.objective: Using price and quantity, create a constant named total equal to price times quantity, then print total.
hints: Multiplication uses the star symbol, and variable names work inside calculations.
Declare const total and set it to price * quantity, then print it.
`const total = price * quantity` then `console.log(total)`
checks: total is calculated from price and quantity

js-template-literals.title: Build a sentence
js-template-literals.summary: Template literals use backticks and ${} to place values inside text. They read more clearly than joining strings with +.
js-template-literals.objective: Create a constant named greeting with a template literal that uses name to produce Hello, Ada! Then print greeting.
hints: Backticks create a string that can hold values inside ${ }.
Write const greeting = followed by a backtick string that contains ${name}.
``const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!` `` then `console.log(greeting)`
checks: greeting uses a template literal with name inside

js-string-methods.title: Clean up text
js-string-methods.summary: Strings come with built-in methods. Chaining them cleans text step by step, and the original string never changes.
js-string-methods.objective: city has extra spaces. Create a constant named clean that trims the spaces and turns the text to uppercase, then print clean.
hints: Methods are called with a dot after a value. Each one returns a new string.
trim() removes the spaces around text and toUpperCase() changes the case. You can chain them.
`const clean = city.trim().toUpperCase()`

js-comparisons.title: Compare values
js-comparisons.summary: Comparisons answer with true or false. Use === to compare values, because == converts types in surprising ways.
js-comparisons.objective: Using age, create isAdult (true when age is 18 or more) and isTwenty (true when age is exactly 20, using ===). Print both.
hints: A comparison is a question that JavaScript answers with true or false.
Use >= for "18 or more" and === for "exactly 20". Store each answer in a constant.
`const isAdult = age >= 18` and `const isTwenty = age === 20`
js-comparisons.commonMistake: == converts types before comparing, so "20" == 20 is true. === compares the type too, which avoids surprises.

js-functions.title: Write a function
js-functions.summary: A function packages steps under a name. Parameters receive input, and return sends a result back to the caller.
js-functions.objective: Write a function named greet that takes a name and returns Hello, then the name and an exclamation mark. greet('Ada') returns Hello, Ada!
hints: A function receives input through parameters and gives back a value with return.
Declare function greet(name) and return a template literal that uses name.
``function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!` }``
js-functions.commonMistake: console.log inside a function only prints. return is what hands the value back to the code that called the function.
checks: greet is declared as a function

js-if-else.title: Make a decision
js-if-else.summary: if runs code only when a condition is true, and else covers every other case. Inside a function, each branch can return its own result.
js-if-else.objective: Write a function named getAdvice that takes a temperature. Return Stay cool when it is above 25, otherwise return Enjoy the sun.
hints: Decide which question to ask about the temperature, then what to answer in each case.
Inside the function, use if (temperature > 25) to return one text, and else to return the other.
`if (temperature > 25) { return 'Stay cool' } else { return 'Enjoy the sun' }`

js-arrow-functions.title: Use a shorter function
js-arrow-functions.summary: Arrow functions are a compact way to write small functions. When the body is one expression, its value is returned automatically.
js-arrow-functions.objective: Create a constant named double that holds an arrow function. It takes a number and returns that number times 2.
hints: An arrow function is a value, so it can be stored in a constant like any other value.
Write const double = (number) => followed by the calculation. One expression needs no braces.
`const double = (number) => number * 2`

js-arrays.title: Make a list
js-arrays.summary: An array holds an ordered list of values. Positions start at 0, and length tells you how many items there are.
js-arrays.objective: Create a constant array named fruits with at least three strings. Print the first item using its index, then print the length.
hints: Arrays use square brackets, with items separated by commas. The first position is 0, not 1.
Declare const fruits with three strings. fruits[0] is the first item and fruits.length is the count.
`console.log(fruits[0])` and `console.log(fruits.length)`
checks: fruits is an array with at least three items
The console shows the first fruit
The console shows how many fruits there are

js-array-push.title: Add to a list
js-array-push.summary: push adds an item to the end of an array. A const array can still change its contents: const only stops the name from pointing elsewhere.
js-array-push.objective: Add the text Practice to the end of tasks with push, then print the length of tasks.
hints: Arrays have methods that change them in place.
Call push on tasks and pass the text Practice.
`tasks.push('Practice')` then `console.log(tasks.length)`
js-array-push.commonMistake: tasks = [...] fails on a const array. push changes the existing array instead of replacing it.
checks: tasks now holds Read and Practice

js-for-loop.title: Repeat with a loop
js-for-loop.summary: A for loop repeats code a set number of times. It has a start, a condition to keep going, and a step.
js-for-loop.objective: Use a for loop to print the numbers 1 to 5, one per line.
hints: A loop needs three parts: where to start, when to stop, and how to move to the next step.
Start a counter at 1, keep going while it is 5 or less, and add 1 each time. Print the counter inside the loop.
`for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { console.log(i) }`
js-for-loop.commonMistake: A condition that never becomes false loops forever. If the preview stops your loop, check that the counter moves toward the end.
checks: Uses a for loop with a counter
The console shows 1 to 5 in order

js-for-of.title: Visit every item
js-for-of.summary: for...of walks through each item of an array without managing an index. It is the clearest loop when you need every value.
js-for-of.objective: Use a for...of loop to print each name in names.
hints: When you need each item and not its position, there is a loop made for that.
Write for (const name of names) and print name inside the loop.
`for (const name of names) { console.log(name) }`
checks: The console shows Ada, Grace, and Linus in order

js-while.title: Loop until done
js-while.summary: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. It fits cases where you do not know the number of steps ahead of time.
js-while.objective: Starting from count = 3, use a while loop to print 3, 2, 1, then print Liftoff! after the loop.
hints: Each pass through the loop must bring the condition closer to false, or it never ends.
Loop while count > 0: print count, then lower it with count--. Print Liftoff! after the closing brace.
`while (count > 0) { console.log(count); count-- }` then `console.log('Liftoff!')`

js-objects.title: Describe a thing
js-objects.summary: An object groups related values under named keys. Dot notation reads a value by its key.
js-objects.objective: Create a constant object named book with a title (text), an author (text), and pages (a number). Print the title with dot notation.
hints: Objects use curly braces, with key: value pairs separated by commas.
Write const book = { title: ..., author: ..., pages: ... }, then print book.title.
`const book = { title: 'Dune', author: 'Frank Herbert', pages: 412 }`
checks: Reads the title with dot notation

js-object-update.title: Update an object
js-object-update.summary: Properties can be changed or added after an object is created, even when the object is a const.
js-object-update.objective: Change the role of user to mentor and add a new property active set to true, without rewriting the object.
hints: Assigning to a property works like assigning to a variable.
Use user.role = ... to change the role, and user.active = ... to add a new key.
`user.role = 'mentor'` and `user.active = true`

js-cart-total.title: Add up a cart
js-cart-total.summary: Loops and objects work well together. A total variable collects a running sum while the loop visits each item.
js-cart-total.objective: Write a function named totalPrice that takes an array of items and returns the sum of their price properties. An empty array returns 0.
hints: Start a total at 0, then add to it once per item.
Inside totalPrice, declare let total = 0, loop over items with for...of, add item.price, then return total.
`let total = 0; for (const item of items) { total += item.price } return total`

js-logical-operators.title: Combine conditions
js-logical-operators.summary: && needs both sides to be true, while || needs only one. They let one line express a whole rule.
js-logical-operators.objective: Write a function named canEnter that takes age and hasTicket. Return true only when age is 18 or more and hasTicket is true.
hints: The rule has two parts that must both be true.
Return age >= 18 combined with hasTicket using &&.
`return age >= 18 && hasTicket`

js-default-params.title: Format a price
js-default-params.summary: Default parameters give a value when the caller leaves one out. toFixed(2) shows a number with two decimals.
js-default-params.objective: Write a function named formatPrice that takes amount and currency, with currency defaulting to EUR. Return the amount with two decimals, a space, then the currency, like 5.00 EUR.
hints: A parameter can have a fallback value written right in the parameter list.
Declare function formatPrice(amount, currency = 'EUR') and use amount.toFixed(2) in a template literal.
``return `${amount.toFixed(2)} ${currency}` ``

js-map.title: Transform every item
js-map.summary: map creates a new array by running a function on each item. The original array stays the same.
js-map.objective: Create a constant named doubled that uses map on numbers to double every value.
hints: map calls your function once per item and collects what it returns.
Call numbers.map with an arrow function that returns the number times 2.
`const doubled = numbers.map((number) => number * 2)`

js-filter.title: Keep what matches
js-filter.summary: filter builds a new array with only the items for which your function returns true.
js-filter.objective: Create a constant named passing with only the scores that are 50 or more, using filter.
hints: filter asks a yes or no question about each item.
Call scores.filter with an arrow function that returns score >= 50.
`const passing = scores.filter((score) => score >= 50)`

js-find-includes.title: Search a list
js-find-includes.summary: find returns the first item that matches, or undefined. includes tells you whether a value is in the array at all.
js-find-includes.objective: Create admin with the first user whose role is admin, using find. Then create hasGuest, true when roles includes guest.
hints: One method returns a matching item, the other returns true or false.
Use users.find with a function that checks user.role === 'admin', and roles.includes('guest').
`const admin = users.find((user) => user.role === 'admin')` and `const hasGuest = roles.includes('guest')`

js-reduce.title: Reduce to one value
js-reduce.summary: reduce walks through an array while carrying a running result. It turns a list into a single value, like a total.
js-reduce.objective: Create a constant named total that uses reduce to add up prices. Start the total at 0.
hints: reduce gives your function the running result and the current item.
Call prices.reduce with (sum, price) => sum + price, and pass 0 as the second argument.
`const total = prices.reduce((sum, price) => sum + price, 0)`
js-reduce.commonMistake: Without a starting value, reduce uses the first item and fails on an empty array. Always pass the starting value.

js-destructuring.title: Unpack values
js-destructuring.summary: Destructuring pulls values out of objects and arrays into variables in one step.
js-destructuring.objective: From movie, destructure title and year into constants. From ranking, destructure the first two items into first and second.
hints: The shape on the left of = mirrors the shape of the value on the right.
Curly braces unpack object keys by name. Square brackets unpack array items by position.
`const { title, year } = movie` and `const [first, second] = ranking`
checks: title is Arrival and year is 2016
first is Ada and second is Grace

js-spread.title: Combine and copy
js-spread.summary: The spread syntax ... copies the items of an array or the keys of an object into a new one, leaving the original untouched.
js-spread.objective: Create allTags by spreading frontend and backend into one new array. Then create updated, a copy of settings with theme set to dark.
hints: Three dots inside brackets or braces copy the contents of another array or object.
Write [...frontend, ...backend] for the array, and { ...settings, theme: 'dark' } for the object.
`const allTags = [...frontend, ...backend]` and `const updated = { ...settings, theme: 'dark' }`
checks: allTags holds all four tags in order
updated has theme dark and keeps fontSize

js-dom-select.title: Change the page
js-dom-select.summary: The DOM is the page as JavaScript sees it. querySelector finds an element with a CSS selector, and textContent changes its text.
js-dom-select.objective: Select the element with the id title and change its text to Hello, DOM!
hints: JavaScript finds elements with the same selectors you use in CSS.
Use document.querySelector('#title') and set its textContent.
`document.querySelector('#title').textContent = 'Hello, DOM!'`

js-dom-class.title: Switch a style
js-dom-class.summary: classList adds and removes CSS classes. Switching classes keeps the look in CSS and the behavior in JavaScript.
js-dom-class.objective: Select the card with the id lesson-card and add the class highlight with classList.
hints: The styles for highlight already exist. Your code only needs to add the class.
Select the card with querySelector, then call classList.add('highlight').
`document.querySelector('#lesson-card').classList.add('highlight')`
js-dom-class.commonMistake: Setting element.style mixes design into your script. Adding a class keeps the design in CSS, where it is easy to change.
checks: The card has the highlight class

js-dom-events.title: Respond to a click
js-dom-events.summary: addEventListener runs a function when something happens, like a click. This is how pages become interactive.
js-dom-events.objective: When the #add button is clicked, increase count by 1 and show the new value in #count.
hints: Keep the count in a variable, then update the page every time it changes.
Call button.addEventListener('click', ...). Inside the function, add 1 to count and write it to output.textContent.
`button.addEventListener('click', () => { count++; output.textContent = count })`

js-dom-create.title: Build a list
js-dom-create.summary: createElement makes a new element and append puts it on the page. Together they turn data into markup.
js-dom-create.objective: For each item in skills, create an li with the skill as its text and append it to the #skills list.
hints: Loop over the data and create one element per item.
Inside a for...of loop, call document.createElement('li'), set its textContent, then list.append(item).
`const item = document.createElement('li'); item.textContent = skill; list.append(item)`
checks: The list shows HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

js-dom-input.title: React to typing
js-dom-input.summary: The input event fires on every keystroke. Reading the field value lets the page react while the person types.
js-dom-input.objective: When someone types in #name, show Hello, then their name and an exclamation mark in #greeting.
hints: Listen for the event that fires while the person types, then read what is in the field.
Use field.addEventListener('input', ...) and read field.value inside the function.
``field.addEventListener('input', () => { greeting.textContent = `Hello, ${field.value}!` })``

js-dom-toggle.title: Open a menu
js-dom-toggle.summary: A toggle flips between two states. Updating aria-expanded along with the class keeps the menu accessible, as in the HTML course.
js-dom-toggle.objective: When #menu-button is clicked, toggle the class open on #menu and set aria-expanded on the button to true or false to match.
hints: The class and the aria-expanded value must always agree.
classList.toggle('open') returns true when it added the class. Pass that value to setAttribute.
`const isOpen = menu.classList.toggle('open'); button.setAttribute('aria-expanded', isOpen)`
checks: A second click closes the menu again

js-form-submit.title: Handle a form
js-form-submit.summary: A submitted form reloads the page by default. preventDefault stops that, so JavaScript can use the data instead.
js-form-submit.objective: When #task-form is submitted, stop the page reload, add the text of #task as a new li in #tasks, then clear the field.
hints: Listen to the form itself, not the button, so pressing Enter works too.
In a submit listener, call event.preventDefault(), create an li from input.value, append it, then set input.value to an empty string.
`form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => { event.preventDefault(); ... })`
checks: The task appears in the list

js-classes.title: Create a class
js-classes.summary: A class is a blueprint for objects that share behavior. The constructor sets the starting state, and methods act on it.
js-classes.objective: Create a class named Counter. Its constructor sets count to 0, and its increment method adds 1 to count and returns the new value.
hints: Inside a class, this refers to the object being created or used.
Inside class Counter, write constructor() { this.count = 0 } and an increment() method.
`increment() { this.count += 1; return this.count }`
checks: Each counter keeps its own count

js-errors.title: Handle errors
js-errors.summary: throw stops a function when something is wrong, and try...catch lets the caller recover instead of crashing.
js-errors.objective: Make parseAge throw an Error when the text is not a number. Then write readAge, which returns parseAge(text), or null when parseAge throws.
hints: Number.isNaN tells you when a conversion to a number failed.
In parseAge, throw new Error(...) when Number.isNaN(age). In readAge, call parseAge inside try and return null in catch.
`try { return parseAge(text) } catch { return null }`

js-json.title: Read and write JSON
js-json.summary: JSON is the text format programs use to exchange data. JSON.parse turns text into values, and JSON.stringify does the opposite.
js-json.objective: Turn text into an object named data with JSON.parse. Then turn settings into a JSON string named output with JSON.stringify.
hints: One method reads JSON text, the other writes it.
Use JSON.parse(text) for data and JSON.stringify(settings) for output.
`const data = JSON.parse(text)` and `const output = JSON.stringify(settings)`
checks: data.name is Ada and data.level is 3
output is the JSON text of settings

js-closures.title: Remember with a closure
js-closures.summary: A function keeps access to the variables around it, even after the outer function has returned. This is called a closure.
js-closures.objective: Write createCounter, which keeps a private count and returns a function. Each call of that function adds 1 and returns the new count.
hints: The inner function can still see the variables of the function that created it.
Inside createCounter, declare let count = 0, then return an arrow function that adds 1 to count and returns it.
`function createCounter() { let count = 0; return () => { count += 1; return count } }`

js-promises.title: Wait with a promise
js-promises.summary: A promise stands for a value that arrives later. Wrapping setTimeout in a promise is the simplest way to see one in action.
js-promises.objective: Write wait(ms), which returns a promise that resolves with the text done after ms milliseconds.
hints: new Promise takes a function that receives resolve. Call resolve when the work is finished.
Return new Promise, and inside it use setTimeout to call resolve('done') after ms.
`return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve('done'), ms))`

js-async-await.title: Await a result
js-async-await.summary: An async function can pause with await until a promise settles. The code still reads from top to bottom.
js-async-await.objective: Write an async function named showScore that awaits getScore(), shows the score in #score, and returns it. Then call showScore().
hints: await only works inside a function marked async.
Declare async function showScore(), then const score = await getScore(). Set the text of #score and return score.
`const score = await getScore(); document.querySelector('#score').textContent = score; return score`

js-capstone.title: Build a to-do list
js-capstone.summary: Bring it all together: events, the DOM, conditions, and state in one small app.
js-capstone.objective: Make the form add trimmed, non-empty tasks to #todos and clear the field. Keep #summary showing 1 task or N tasks. Clicking a task toggles the class done.
hints: Solve it in small steps: add tasks first, then clear the field, then the summary, then the click.
In the submit listener: preventDefault, trim the value, stop if it is empty, create an li with its own click listener, append it, clear the field, and update the summary.
``const count = list.children.length; summary.textContent = count === 1 ? '1 task' : `${count} tasks` ``
checks: The task is added without extra spaces
The summary says 2 tasks after a second task
Clicking a task marks it done
